newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia oilmen vote to strike if talks fail.
newsitem.headline: Colombia oilmen vote to strike if talks fail.

text.p: Colombia's main oil workers' union voted Monday to strike in protest over the arrest of 11 members on terrorism charges, but leaders said the walkout would be put on hold pending more emergency talks with the government.
The widely expected decision, taken at a meeting in the northern oil production centre of Barrancabermeja, means the USO union will begin preparations for an indefinite strike.
But the strike will begin only if meetings with government ministers starting on Sunday fail, said USO social services secretary Gustavo Triana.
"As predicted, USO members voted to strike and authorised the national directorate to set the zero hour. The resolution also allowed for the continuation of talks with the government," Triana said.
"That means we will not intiate the stoppage until we feel that talks with the government have failed," he added.
USO head Hernando Hernandez said production would be scaled down in the lead-up to an all-out strike.

Fourteen men, 11 of them USO members, have been arrested since Thursday on charges of dynamiting oil pipelines and having links to the National Liberation Army, Colombia's second largest guerrilla force.
USO leaders will meet with private sector oil workers on Tuesday to try to persuade them to heed the strike call if the talks collapse, Triana said.

Following a merger with smaller industry associations two months ago, the 5,700-strong USO has expanded beyond the state-run oil company Ecopetrol to the private sector, including foreign multinationals.

In addition to trying to hammer out an agreement on the fate of the detainees in meetings with the interior, defense, mines and energy, and labor ministers later this week, the USO will be seeking guarantees that Ecopetrol will not be carved up.

The USO has accused the government of creeping privatisation plans for the state oil company. It fears splitting the company into separate gas, oil and refining operations would loosen its grip on labor.

Mines and Energy Minister Rodrigo Villamizar said plans had been laid to ensure fuel supplies do not run low in the event of a strike. Existing stocks would last for almost three weeks and imports would be increased if necessary, he said.
